transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Cruz (Redwood SE), Jared Liu (CTO, StratusAI), Maya Thompson (SRE), Alicia Perez (Platform Eng)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to align on observability integration approach for Redwood's inference runtime. Focus areas: OpenTelemetry collector integration, token-level metrics and how we expose latency/throughput and KV cache metrics, dashboards for SRE/Prod, and what pilot benchmarks StratusAI will run (KV cache + batching + quantization).

Topics (auto): Open Telemetry setup, spans vs metrics, token metrics instrumentation, exporter config, Grafana dashboard templates, on-prem/VPC restrictions, audit logs for traces

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'll hand it over to Elena to kick off the technical parts. Uh, hi Jared, Maya, Alicia.
[00:08] Elena Cruz: Hi, thanks. So today we want to walk through how Redwood integrates with OpenTelemetry and what token-level metrics look like. We'll also show what we recommend for collecting traces in VPC/private deployments — and how to surface KV cache and batching stats.
[00:24] Jared Liu: Great. We're especially interested in token-level latency, how caching shows up, and minimal on-prem collector changes.
[00:31] Elena Cruz: Totally understood. Quick note, some of the auto-transcribe may flip words, you'll hear "KV" as K V sometimes.
[00:37] Maya Thompson: haha okay fair.
[00:40] Elena Cruz: First, architecture. Redwood emits both metrics and tracing signals. Metrics: Prom-style counters/gauges for token emit rate, per-model token latency histograms, batching sizes, in-flight requests, and cache hit/miss counters for our KV cache. Traces: we create spans per request lifecycle — from front-end ingestion through routing, model exec, and response assembly. We also attach tokenization and per-token generation timing as span attributes.
[01:07] Jared Liu: When you say "per-token generation timing" — is that like a separate span per token? That could blow up traces, right?
[01:13] Elena Cruz: Good question. We typically don't create a full span per token by default because of volume; instead we emit a compact representation: a token-level timing histogram or a sampled set of per-token timings as attributes. In heavy sampling mode we can emit per-token spans, but that's opt-in.
[01:28] Alicia Perez: If we enable per-token spans in our VPC deployment, what are the storage implications? We have limited trace retention.
[01:35] Elena Cruz: Right — so that's why we recommend a hybrid approach: metrics for roll-ups (token rate, p50/p95/p99 per-token latency), and sampled traces for deep debugging. If you need full per-token traces for specific flows, we suggest targeted sampling rules.
[01:47] Samir Patel: I'll add that our Redwood Optimize team also provides suggestions for which prompts to sample to catch regressions without huge trace volume.

[02:00] Maya Thompson: Can you show the OTEL collector config you recommend? We're running an on-prem collector forwarder to our internal observability.
[02:07] Elena Cruz: Yep, Elena shares a config in the meeting chat (link). The recommended pattern is: Redwood exports OTLP/gRPC to your collector; the collector applies attribute enrichments and forwards metrics to Prom remote_write or traces to your tracing backend. For on-prem we also support direct push to an internal OpenTelemetry endpoint if you expose one through the VPC peering.
[02:29] Jared Liu: Any special auth? Our security team requires mTLS and tokens.
[02:33] Elena Cruz: We can do mTLS or bearer tokens. For private deployments we support customer-managed certs. The OTLP exporter we provide can be configured with client certs. We'll send the sample snippet.
[02:44] Alicia Perez: Are there examples for Grafana dashboards for token-level metrics? We want p50/p95/p99 charts and a heatmap for token latency distributions.
[02:52] Elena Cruz: Yes, we have a starter Grafana dashboard template — shows per-model token latency histograms, cache hit ratio over time, batching size distribution, and a trace link panel that opens traces in your APM. We'll drop the JSON. It also includes token-level rate and quota usage.
[03:06] Samir Patel: I'll note here that Datadog and Honeycomb customers we onboard often map the same metrics but with slightly different names; we include a mapping table in the doc.

[03:20] [SCREEN SHARE: Elena shows dashboard mockup]
[03:26] Elena Cruz: On this dashboard, left side is model-level latency — histogram-based bucketed metrics for per-token timings. Middle is batching and queueing: average batch size, batch wait time, and in-flight batches. Right side is cache: hit rate, miss latency, and eviction counts.
[03:42] Maya Thompson: For batch wait time, what is the unit? ms per batch or ms per token?
[03:46] Elena Cruz: It's ms per batch wait; we also compute normalized per-token wait time. In our metrics we emit both batch_wait_ms and batch_wait_per_token_ms.
[03:54] Jared Liu: Does your runtime emit KV cache latency per key lookup? We need to understand tail latencies when cache misses go to slower storage.
[04:01] Elena Cruz: Yes — cache_lookup_duration_ms histogram, plus labels for cache_tier (in-memory/local, remote-redis, s3) so you can break out tail latencies by tier.

[04:15] Alicia Perez: If we're running Redwood Private in our VPC, are you asking us to run the OTEL collector inside the VPC? We prefer to have the collector already in our monitoring stack.
[04:24] Samir Patel: That's fine — Redwood can be configured to send OTLP directly to your collector endpoint; no internet egress needed if you route via peering. For air-gapped on-prem, we can handshake with your ops team for the safe cert exchange.

[04:40] Elena Cruz: A note on sampling: we support route-level sampling policies so you can always sample 100% for a selected set of endpoints (e.g., high business-critical flows) and sample at lower rates elsewhere. We also include contextual sampling — e.g., sample more when latency spikes are observed.
[04:57] Maya Thompson: How do you detect latency spikes? Is that observed on token-level metrics or aggregate request latency?
[05:02] Elena Cruz: Both. We compute rolling windows on token-level histograms and request latencies. Our anomaly detector in the console can trigger higher sampling when metrics exceed configured thresholds.

[05:18] Jared Liu: On the topic of quantization and kernel selection: do you expose model execution stage timing? We want to know time spent in quantized kernel versus dequantization overhead.
[05:27] Elena Cruz: Yes, we expose execution_stage_ms with labels for stage=kernel_exec, stage=dequantize, stage=kvcache_lookup, etc. For quantized models, you'll see smaller kernel_exec times but sometimes increased dequantization cost — we show that breakdown.
[05:40] Alicia Perez: Is dequantization done per-token or per-chunk?
[05:43] Elena Cruz: Per-chunk — depending on model and implementation. We add attributes for chunk_size so you can correlate.

[05:51] Samir Patel: Quick aside — regarding storage for metrics: if you push to your Prom remote_write, you'll control retention. We also offer a managed metrics endpoint as an add-on for Dedicated customers.

[06:05] [15 minute mark check-in]
[06:08] Maya Thompson: Sorry, quick question about trace sampling and PII: we need to ensure token text for certain flows is never sent out. Can you mask tokens in spans/attributes?
[06:20] Elena Cruz: Absolutely. We support attribute redaction and can avoid including token text entirely on traces. By default we only attach token latency or token index, not token raw text. If you want token text for debug, that's opt-in and has to be approved.

[06:35] Jared Liu: Okay that's critical for compliance.

[06:38] Elena Cruz: Going back to instrumentation — let me describe a typical metric naming convention: redwood.runtime.{model}.{metric_name} with labels model, region, deployment_id, route. Examples: redwood.runtime.gpt-xx.token_latency_bucket, redwood.runtime.gpt-xx.kv_cache_hits_total.
[06:55] Jared Liu: Will those names be configurable? Our SREs want a prefix to match existing conventions.
[06:59] Elena Cruz: Yes, prefix and label names can be mapped in the exporter. We include a mapping table in the doc we shared.

[07:08] Maya Thompson: For alerting, what's the recommended SLO signals? We care about p99 token latency translating into request-level p99 SLA.
[07:16] Elena Cruz: Recommended signals: p99 token latency, median batch size, queue depth, cache_miss_rate. We also suggest instrumenting end-to-end request latency and synthetic probes for cold starts. We can provide a promql set for SLO: e.g., 1 - sum(rate(redwood_runtime_request_latency_bucket{le="<threshold>"}[5m])) / sum(rate(redwood_runtime_request_latency_count[5m])). We'll share snippets.

[07:43] Samir Patel: Now on KV cache visibility — we'll often surface hit ratio by route and model, and also provide a dependent heatmap showing keys with high miss rates. That helps ops target eviction policies.

[07:57] Alicia Perez: Do you handle correlations between prompt size and cache effectiveness?
[08:01] Elena Cruz: Yes — we emit prompt_length_bucket and pair it with cache_hit boolean so you can correlate.

[08:10] [Screen: example tracer view]
[08:15] Elena Cruz: Here's a trace for a long streaming request. You can see spans for tokenizer, KV lookup (miss), batch wait, kernel execute, and streaming assembly. The trace links to logs and the dashboard shows token-level latency spikes.

[08:33] Jared Liu: Regarding logs — do you also emit structured logs with trace_id so we can join logs and traces?
[08:38] Elena Cruz: Yes, we propagate trace_id and span_id into logs. If you're shipping logs to a central system, you can correlate easily. We also include request_id at the top level.

[08:48] Maya Thompson: For large customers we sometimes want to run distributed tracing without exposing internal hostnames. Does Redwood respect hostname obfuscation?
[08:55] Elena Cruz: We can redact hostnames and use opaque instance IDs. For Private deployments we also can configure what metadata is sent.

[09:05] Jared Liu: One of our main questions: how will we benchmark KV cache effectiveness + batching? We want to simulate production load.

[09:13] Elena Cruz: We recommend a two-phase pilot: Phase A — capture a representative traffic sample (you provide traces or request logs) and we run our offline simulator to estimate expected cache hit rates and batching profiles; Phase B — run an instrumented pilot on Dedicated or Private with controlled traffic to measure end-to-end tokens/sec, p95/p99 latencies, and cost. We'll help set up the workload generator or run it jointly.

[09:36] Samir Patel: For the pilot we'll need: your sample request traffic, target SLAs, and any particular models/quantization configs you want to test.

[09:44] Alicia Perez: We plan to test a q8_0 quantized variant and a full-fp16 baseline. We'll share model sizes and expected seq lengths.

[09:51] Elena Cruz: Perfect — quantization results will show up in kernel_exec_ms and memory footprint metrics. We also report throughput tokens/sec and GPU utilization on Dedicated.

[10:03] Maya Thompson: On telemetry retention — if we are sampling heavily for a short pilot, can Redwood provide a short-lived higher retention window to capture all pilot traces?
[10:12] Elena Cruz: Yes, for pilots we can bump retention or stream to your storage for the pilot window. We'll coordinate via the pilot run doc.

[10:20] Jared Liu: Are there any known gotchas with OTLP/gRPC to our collector in VPC peering? We had issues with connection resets in the past.
[10:27] Elena Cruz: Two things to watch: keepalive settings and batch sizes on exporter. For high-throughput OTLP we recommend configuring exporter keepalive ping to avoid TCP timeouts and using compression for large payloads. Also ensure your collector has sufficient ingest threads. We'll provide recommended settings.

[10:44] Samir Patel: I'd like to circle back to dashboards — we'll send a Grafana template. Do you want it in JSON or as a Helm chart?
[10:51] Alicia Perez: JSON is fine, we can import it into our Grafana. If you have a Helm chart we can evaluate too.

[10:58] Elena Cruz: We'll attach the JSON and the PromQL and trace link templates.

[11:03] [15:00 minute mark — discussion continues deeper on KV cache internals]
[11:08] Elena Cruz: Internals: our KV cache is sharded per-GPU and has adaptive TTLs; we emit per-shard metrics including shard_size_bytes, eviction_count, and read_latency_ms. For remote caches we include network latency as a metric.

[11:21] Maya Thompson: Could you expose per-key miss patterns in a table? That's expensive to compute.

[11:25] Elena Cruz: We don't do full per-key retention at full volume by default, because of cost; instead we sample keys with high miss rates and export hot-key reports. We can enable more aggressive key telemetry for pilots.

[11:38] Jared Liu: About batching — do you support request-level hints to force small batches for low-latency flows?

[11:45] Elena Cruz: Yes, you can set route-level policies: prefer_low_latency which biases dispatching to smaller batches, or prefer_throughput which allows larger batches. We emit metrics to show the effective batch size and the tradeoff on latency.

[11:58] Alicia Perez: We'll likely want prefer_low_latency for our real-time chat but prefer_throughput for large offline scoring.

[12:05] Elena Cruz: Exactly — and the console can do A/B rollout between those policies.

[12:12] Samir Patel: Any questions about security/audit for traces?

[12:16] Maya Thompson: Yes — our security team will ask: who can query traces, and do you log access to trace data?

[12:22] Elena Cruz: For Redwood-hosted telemetry we include RBAC controls and audit logs for trace access. For Private deployments, audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM.

[12:33] Jared Liu: On the point of correlation keys — what labels are required to join logs/metrics/traces?

[12:38] Elena Cruz: We propagate request_id, trace_id, model, deployment_id, and route. We recommend also adding customer_user_id if present for application-level correlation (but that's optional).

[12:51] [20 minute check-in — audience asks for clarifications]
[12:55] Maya Thompson: If we want to sample traces more aggressively during an incident, can we flip sampling remotely?

[12:59] Elena Cruz: Yes, sampling policies can be dynamically updated via the control plane and take effect in seconds. You can also set triggers to auto-escalate sampling when an anomaly is detected.

[13:12] Jared Liu: For pilot success criteria — what metrics should we agree on?

[13:18] Samir Patel: Suggested criteria: end-to-end p95 under X ms (you define X), cache hit rate over Y% for the targeted workload, and tokens/sec throughput meeting your target. Also observability completeness: ability to link traces to metric anomalies and reproduce a failing trace.

[13:33] Alicia Perez: We'll draft target numbers and send them.

[13:37] Elena Cruz: One more operational note: when running on-prem, you may prefer to only accept metrics (no traces) initially. That's fine — the integration is incremental.

[13:47] Maya Thompson: Regarding the dashboard that shows kernel-level timings, how granular are the histograms? Bucket count?

[13:53] Elena Cruz: We use exponential buckets tuned for ms-level timings, default 50 buckets; configurable. For token timings we capture high-resolution in the 0.1ms to 5000ms range depending on model.

[14:05] Jared Liu: You mentioned trace links to logs — do you provide a direct link format for our Splunk/Datadog?

[14:10] Elena Cruz: Yes, we provide templates for most common backends; we'll include examples for Datadog and Honeycomb in the doc.

[14:18] Samir Patel: Let's capture next steps — I'll run through them and we can confirm.

[14:22] Samir Patel: Action item recap: Elena will send OTEL collector example and Grafana JSON; Samir will share pilot pricing and options; Maya will provide sample traffic and desired SLAs; Elena will prepare recommended OTLP exporter settings for VPC peering. Any additions?

[14:38] Jared Liu: Please also include the mapping table for metric names for Datadog/Prometheus.

[14:43] Samir Patel: Noted. Any other blockers?

[14:46] Maya Thompson: Nothing else from SRE right now.

[14:49] Alicia Perez: We're good, thanks.

[14:52] Elena Cruz: Great — we'll follow up in the next couple days with docs and artifacts. Thanks all.

[14:58] Samir Patel: Thanks everyone — talk soon.

End of transcript.
